modules.title: 01. Files, processes and the command line
modules.description: Build a usable mental model of local computing before programming. Work only in a new learner-owned scratch directory. Prior job exposure is context, not evidence that these outcomes are already mastered.

lessons.title: Distinguish files, running programs and execution context
objectives: Resolve an absolute and a relative path to the same learner-created file.
Explain the difference between a program stored on disk, its running process and its current working directory.
Identify and interrupt only a harmless process started for the exercise.

topics.title: Files and paths
details: Directories, file extensions, text versus bytes, current directory and path quoting.
A relative path depends on execution context; a file can remain after the program that created it exits.

topics.title: Processes and resources
details: A process has an identity, lifetime, working directory and inherited environment.
An executable on disk is not the same thing as its running process; output and errors are separate observations.

topics.title: Safe local navigation
details: Bash and PowerShell have different commands and syntax; PowerShell equivalents include Get-Location, Get-ChildItem and Get-Content.
Inspect before acting; no administrator commands, account changes, profile edits or broad process termination.

video.locator: 2020 lecture Course Overview + The Shell: What is the shell?, Using the shell, and Navigating in the shell. Also use the supplementary Command-line Environment lecture's Job Control portion.

reading.locator: GNU Bash Reference Manual 5.3: section 1.2 What is a shell? and sections 3.7.2 Command Search and Execution and 3.7.3 Command Execution Environment. Read the prose for the mental model, not all advanced shell features.

assignment.title: Map and observe a disposable workspace
instructions: Budget about 90 minutes for this assignment, included in the lesson estimate. Choose an installed shell and create a new empty practice directory, not an existing repository.
Create two nested directories, including one with a space in its name, and two short text files containing invented labels. Draw their directory tree.
Read one file by an absolute path and by a relative path from two different current directories. Record which relative path changes and why.
Start a harmless waiting subprocess using your shell's documented method, record its PID, observe it, and interrupt only that subprocess. Do not terminate by process name or modify system settings.
Write a six-sentence explanation separating the shell, the subprocess, its working directory, the program file and the text files.
deliverables: Directory-tree sketch and a short command transcript without personal paths outside the practice directory.
Path-resolution table for the two working directories.
PID observation and the six-sentence explanation.
acceptanceCriteria: Both path forms read identical file contents, and the transcript demonstrates two distinct current directories.
At least one path containing spaces is handled correctly.
The learner identifies the process they started and records its termination without affecting another process.
The explanation correctly distinguishes persistent files from a running process and contains no claim that a filename extension alone proves file contents.

reviewPrompts: Why can the same relative path refer to different files in two terminals?
What remains on disk after a process exits, and what may be lost?
How would you establish that a PID belongs to your exercise before interrupting it?

lessons.title: Compose commands without hiding errors
objectives: Build a small filter, sort and deduplication workflow over a text fixture.
Separate standard output from standard error and inspect command success.
Explain quoting, overwrite versus append, and why a pipeline can hide an earlier failure.

topics.title: Arguments and quoting
details: Commands receive arguments; spaces and metacharacters can change how those arguments are parsed.
Use shell-specific quoting rather than pasting Bash redirections into PowerShell unchanged.

topics.title: Streams and composition
details: Standard input, output and error; filtering, sorting, unique values and counting.
Overwrite and append have different effects; preserve the original input fixture.

topics.title: Visible failure
details: Check native exit status or the chosen shell's documented error mechanism.
Bash normally reports the last pipeline command's status unless pipefail is enabled; do not turn a missing input into a successful empty report.

video.locator: Course Overview + The Shell: Using the shell and Connecting programs; revisit the lecture's redirection and pipe demonstrations.

reading.locator: Sections 3.1.2 Quoting, 3.2.3 Pipelines, 3.6.1 Redirecting Input, 3.6.2 Redirecting Output and 3.6.3 Appending Redirected Output.

assignment.title: Produce a tiny log summary with a failure case
instructions: Budget about 90 minutes. In the practice directory, create an eight-line fixture: INFO alpha; ERROR beta; INFO gamma; ERROR beta; WARN delta; ERROR epsilon; INFO zeta; WARN eta, with each entry on its own line.
Use your selected shell's text tools to select ERROR lines, count them, and produce a sorted list of distinct ERROR lines. Keep raw counts distinct from deduplicated counts.
Save normal output and error output separately. Demonstrate append and overwrite on a disposable output file, not on the input.
Repeat with an intentionally nonexistent input path. Make the failure observable and prevent a success-shaped empty summary. Record the shell-specific error/status check.
Explain each stage in your own words and keep all commands scoped to the practice directory.
deliverables: Input fixture, command sequence and output files.
A failure transcript and explanation of the status check.
A five-line explanation of quoting, pipes and redirection.
acceptanceCriteria: The input has eight lines, three ERROR lines and two distinct ERROR lines.
The distinct output contains ERROR beta followed by ERROR epsilon.
The source fixture remains unchanged after all demonstrations.
The missing-input run is explicitly reported as failed, not as zero errors found.

reviewPrompts: When does a pipe carry error output, and when does it not?
What is the difference between an empty valid input and an input that could not be opened?
Why can checking only the final pipeline stage be misleading?

modules.title: 02. Python values, contracts, collections and modules
modules.description: Make Python the common implementation language. Move beyond exposure by writing and explaining small programs, explicit contracts, collection transformations and importable file-based tools. Advanced object-oriented design and frameworks are not prerequisites.

lessons.title: Trace values and choose the correct branch
objectives: Predict the values and types produced by short expressions before running them.
Implement mutually exclusive branches with explicit boundary behavior.
Explain assignment, comparison, Boolean logic and numeric conversion without treating them as interchangeable.

topics.title: Values and statements
details: Integers, floats, strings, Booleans and None; variables bind names to objects.
Arithmetic, comparison, conversion, evaluation order and the distinction between = and ==.

topics.title: Branching
details: if, elif, else, compound conditions and boundary cases.
Trace one path through a program; a branch condition is not evidence that an unrelated case was handled.

topics.title: Executable reasoning
details: Predict, run, compare and explain a mismatch instead of changing code until a sample happens to pass.
Numeric representation is introduced here; detailed floating-point limitations are developed in module 06.

video.locator: CS50P Week 1 - Conditionals: if, elif, else, or, and and bool. First use the supplementary Week 0 - Functions lecture's Variables, int, float and Operators topics if unfamiliar.

reading.locator: Chapter 1 Programming as a way of thinking; Chapter 2 Variables and Statements; the conditionals and Boolean-expression material in Chapter 5 Conditionals and Recursion. Recursion and the book's exercises are not required here.

assignment.title: Classify a fictional practice-session duration
instructions: Budget about 150 minutes. Write a script of at most 40 nonblank lines that reads integer actual_minutes and target_minutes and prints exactly one classification.
Require actual_minutes to be nonnegative and target_minutes to be positive. For valid inputs print below-target, equal-target or over-target; for an invalid numeric range print invalid-range.

Before running, predict the output for (0,30), (29,30), (30,30), (31,30), (1,0), (-1,30), (10,-2) and (120,60). This lesson's test domain is integer input; friendly handling of malformed text is developed next.
Run all eight cases, record actual output, and explain any correction. Include six additional expression predictions covering a string, integer, float, Boolean, conversion and None.
Do not connect these fictional labels to learning-platform completion or real personal study records.
deliverables: The script and eight-case prediction/observation table.
Six expression predictions with observed types and values.
A short explanation of branch ordering and boundary choices.
acceptanceCriteria: All eight specified cases match the written contract and print exactly one classification each.
Zero actual minutes is valid when the target is positive; zero or negative targets are rejected.
The equal case cannot also be labelled below or over target.
Predictions are distinguished from observations; the artifact does not invent a successful run.

reviewPrompts: What changes when a number is stored as a string?
How can reordering branches change boundary behavior?
Why is a missing value different from zero and from an empty string?

lessons.title: Write functions with explicit success and failure contracts
objectives: Separate input/output from reusable calculation and validation functions.
Document accepted inputs, return values and expected exceptions.
Read a traceback and catch only an exception that the caller can meaningfully handle.

topics.title: Function boundaries
details: Parameters, arguments, local scope, return values and side effects.
A printed value is not a returned value; every intended success path must return the promised type.

topics.title: Contracts and decomposition
details: State input domains, output meaning, units and invalid-input behavior.
Build and check a small function incrementally before adding another responsibility.

topics.title: Exceptions
details: Syntax errors versus runtime exceptions; ValueError, TypeError and useful traceback context.
Use narrow exception handling at the interface; do not silently replace invalid input with a plausible result.

video.locator: CS50P Week 0 - Functions: def, parameters, scope and return. Pair with the supplementary Week 3 - Exceptions topics ValueError, try/except and raise.

reading.locator: Chapter 3 Functions and Chapter 6 Return Values, especially 6.1 Some functions have return values, 6.2 And some have None, 6.3 Return values and conditionals, and 6.4 Incremental development.

assignment.title: Build a duration parser with a real contract
instructions: Budget about 135 minutes. Implement parse_seconds(text), accepting a string containing an integer after surrounding whitespace is removed, and returning an integer between 0 and 7200 inclusive.

Raise ValueError for malformed or out-of-range text. Implement classify_seconds(seconds), returning short below 60, standard from 60 through 300, and long above 300, for the same valid numeric domain.
Give both functions concise contract docstrings. Keep terminal input and output outside the functions, and show an actionable message for expected bad input.
Check at least ten calls, including '0', ' 60 ', '300', '301', '7200', '-1', '7201', 'later', '1.5' and the empty string. Use the Python manual's chapter 8 Errors and Exceptions for handling syntax.
Retain one deliberately caused traceback and explain its exception type, relevant line and root cause before fixing the code.
deliverables: Two functions, a thin command-line wrapper and contract docstrings.
Ten input/expected-result checks, including expected exceptions.
A traceback explanation and the corresponding correction.
acceptanceCriteria: Successful parse results are integers; 0 and 7200 are accepted and both out-of-range neighbors are rejected.
The classification boundaries at 59, 60, 300 and 301 are correct.
Malformed text raises ValueError in the parser rather than returning zero or None.
Importing the functions does not prompt or print, and exception handling does not use a blanket catch to hide unrelated bugs.

reviewPrompts: What should a caller know without reading the function body?
Why is print not a replacement for return?
Where should an expected validation error become a user-facing message?

lessons.title: Transform collections without losing meaning
objectives: Select an appropriate list, tuple, dictionary or set for a small problem.
Write an explicit iteration and a readable equivalent transformation where appropriate.
Demonstrate the difference between aliasing, copying and mutation.

topics.title: Container semantics
details: Ordered sequences, dictionary keys and values, distinct set members and immutable tuples.
Membership, indexing, slicing, iteration and missing keys; absence is not automatically a zero value.

topics.title: Iteration
details: for and while, range, enumerate-style index/value reasoning, accumulation and termination.
Prefer a clear loop to a dense comprehension when validation or several updates are required.

topics.title: Object identity and mutation
details: Two names can reference the same mutable object; shallow copies still share nested objects.
Separate an input fixture from output collections and state whether input mutation is allowed.

video.locator: CS50P Week 2 - Loops: while, for, list, range, len, dict and None.

reading.locator: Chapter 7 Iteration and Search; Chapter 9 Lists; Chapter 10 Dictionaries; Chapter 11 Tuples. Read the explanatory container and iteration material, not every chapter exercise. Use Python Tutorial chapter 5 Data Structures for sets.

assignment.title: Summarize five synthetic observations
instructions: Budget about 150 minutes. Represent the original synthetic observations (A,1), (B,5), (A,3), (B,None), (C,0) as dictionaries in a list.
Write summarize(records), returning each station's row count, nonmissing-value count and sum of nonmissing values, plus the set of distinct station labels.
Keep None separate from zero. Preserve the original records unchanged and explicitly sort station labels only when presenting the result.

Add an empty-input case and at least three additional small fixtures. Demonstrate aliasing and a shallow copy using a separate disposable nested list, then explain why the inner object is still shared.
Write a short justification for the container chosen for each part; do not add a class hierarchy or a data-processing framework.
deliverables: The summarizer and at least five fixture checks.
A deterministic human-readable output for the specified fixture.
An aliasing demonstration and container-choice explanation.
acceptanceCriteria: A has row count 2, value count 2 and sum 4; B has row count 2, value count 1 and sum 5; C has row count 1, value count 1 and sum 0.
Distinct labels are A, B and C, while the original five records remain unchanged.
Empty input returns an explicitly documented empty summary without dividing by zero.
The learner can show why filtering values by truthiness would incorrectly discard the valid zero.

reviewPrompts: When is a set the wrong choice even if you want fast membership tests?
What does a shallow copy fail to isolate?
How would you preserve both missingness and a legitimate zero while aggregating?

lessons.title: Turn a script into a repeatable local tool
objectives: Split a small program into an importable module and a command-line entry point.
Read a text file with explicit encoding and resource cleanup.
Create an isolated environment and identify the interpreter actually running the program.

topics.title: Modules and entry points
details: import, module namespaces, the search path and the __name__ guard.
Keep imports free of prompting, network calls and file writes; distinguish the standard library from installed packages.

topics.title: Local file input
details: with and open, UTF-8 text, line boundaries and file-not-found errors.
Pass paths as arguments rather than hardcoding a personal directory or relying on a notebook's hidden state.

topics.title: Environments
details: An environment belongs to a particular interpreter; python -m pip targets that interpreter.
A standard-library-only tool needs no third-party packages. On Windows the environment's Scripts\python.exe can be invoked directly without changing execution policy or profiles.

video.locator: CS50P Week 4 - Libraries: Modules, import, Command-Line Arguments, sys.argv, sys.exit, Packages, pip and __name__. Virtual environments are in the reading.

reading.locator: Tutorial chapter 6 Modules, especially 6.1.1 Executing modules as scripts and 6.1.2 The Module Search Path; section 7.2 Reading and Writing Files; chapter 12 Virtual Environments and Packages.

assignment.title: Package a small text-summary command
instructions: Budget about 120 minutes. Create text_summary.py with a reusable function and main.py with an entry-point guard. Count lines and whitespace-separated words in a UTF-8 file supplied as an argument.
Use only the standard library, a with block for file access, and a useful stderr message plus nonzero exit status for a missing file or argument.
Create a virtual environment and record sys.executable and the Python version. On Windows call its Scripts\python.exe directly if activation is unavailable.
Create a three-line fixture containing six words in total, plus a separate empty fixture. Run from two current directories using appropriate paths.
Import text_summary in a fresh interpreter and show that no input prompt, output or file write occurs.
deliverables: Two Python files, two original text fixtures and a short usage note.
Interpreter/environment identity and exact run commands.
Normal, empty-input and missing-file observations.
acceptanceCriteria: The designed three-line fixture reports three lines and six words; the empty fixture reports zero of each.
Both working-directory runs produce the same counts for the same file.
Invalid invocation and missing files produce explicit errors and nonzero status, not a successful empty summary.
The module is safe to import, and all recorded execution uses the intended isolated interpreter.

reviewPrompts: What code executes when a module is imported?
Why can pip and python refer to different installations?
Why should the file path be an input instead of a hardcoded personal location?

modules.title: 03. Relational data, SQL and trustworthy inputs
modules.description: Use Python's local SQLite support and a tiny synthetic station-reading dataset to establish relational reasoning, basic querying and provenance. SQL/PySpark/Fabric work exposure does not initialize this module as mastered. No PostgreSQL transactions, warehouses or distributed data systems are required.

lessons.title: Give every row a clear meaning
objectives: State the grain of each table and identify its primary and foreign keys.
Explain a one-to-many relationship and predict join cardinality.
Create a tiny schema that rejects duplicate keys and unknown references.

topics.title: Relational vocabulary
details: Relation/table, row, column, domain and row grain.
A conceptual relation has distinct tuples, but SQL tables need appropriate constraints; query output is not inherently ordered.

topics.title: Keys and relationships
details: Stable identifiers, primary-key uniqueness, foreign-key references and one-to-many cardinality.
Separate station descriptions from repeated measurements instead of duplicating descriptive fields in every row.

topics.title: Small, explicit constraints
details: Required identifiers, allowed missing temperature and a bounded numeric domain.
Enable SQLite foreign-key enforcement on the connection before inserts and verify that it is enabled.

video.locator: CS50 SQL Week 1 - Relating: Relational Databases, Relationships, Entity Relationship Diagrams, Primary Keys and Foreign Keys.

reading.locator: Chapter 7 The Relational Data Model: Fundamental Concepts in the Relational Data Model and Properties of a Table. Keys and concrete SQLite enforcement are supplied by the lecture and supplementary official references.

assignment.title: Model three fictional stations and six readings
instructions: Budget about 120 minutes. Draw two tables: stations(station_id, label) and readings(reading_id, station_id, minute_index, temperature_c). State one-row meaning, keys, units and nullability.
Use stations S1, S2 and S3 with invented labels. Use readings (r1,S1,0,18), (r2,S1,5,20), (r3,S1,10,NULL), (r4,S2,0,22), (r5,S2,5,24), (r6,S2,10,26). S3 intentionally has no readings.

Create the schema in a new local SQLite database using Python sqlite3. Identifiers and minute_index are required; minute_index must be an integer from 0 through 59. Temperature may be NULL or a number from -20 through 60.
Enable and check PRAGMA foreign_keys before inserts. Use bound parameters for data values, with the Python manual's sqlite3 placeholder guidance.
Attempt a duplicate reading ID, an unknown station and a missing required station ID. Keep these attempts separate from the six-row clean fixture and record the expected constraint failures.
deliverables: Two-table diagram and a short data dictionary.
Schema and original fixture-loading code.
Evidence of the three rejected insert attempts and the foreign-key setting.
acceptanceCriteria: Exactly three station rows and six clean reading rows remain after the rejection checks.
Primary keys reject duplicate IDs and foreign-key enforcement rejects an unknown station.
The missing temperature on r3 is valid, while a missing station_id is not.
The learner predicts that an inner join returns six reading rows and explains why S3 disappears from that result.

reviewPrompts: What question tells you the grain of a table?
Why is declaring a SQLite foreign key not enough by itself?
When can joining two tables multiply rows unexpectedly?

objectives: Write filtering, ordering, join and grouping queries over the six-row fixture.
Distinguish WHERE from HAVING and COUNT(*) from a count of nonmissing values.
Validate query output against a small independent expected-result table.

details: SELECT, WHERE, comparison predicates, IS NULL, DISTINCT and explicit ORDER BY.
NULL is not zero and is not equal to another value through ordinary equality.

topics.title: Joins and aggregation
details: INNER JOIN versus LEFT JOIN, grouped COUNT and AVG, and HAVING.
In a left join, COUNT(reading_id) avoids counting a placeholder row as a real observation.

topics.title: Correctness before scale
details: Predict result grain and cardinality before running a query.
Use SQLite documentation for executable dialect details; do not copy SQL Server-specific textbook syntax.

assignment.title: Create six independently checkable queries
instructions: Budget about 150 minutes. Reuse the six clean readings from the preceding lesson and write six queries: temperatures at least 22; total versus nonmissing temperature counts; missing-temperature IDs; an inner join to station labels; a per-station left-join summary; and stations having at least three readings.

Write expected rows by hand before executing. Add explicit ordering wherever output order is part of your check.

Explain a deliberately wrong left-join COUNT(*) result and correct it without deleting the empty station.

Hand-derived expected outputs and actual-output comparisons.
A short explanation of NULL, HAVING and the left-join counting trap.

The reading table has total count 6, measured count 5 and exactly one missing-temperature ID, r3.
S1 reports 3 readings, 2 measured values and mean 19; S2 reports 3, 3 and mean 24; S3 reports 0, 0 and a NULL mean.
The inner join has six rows, and the HAVING query returns S1 and S2 only.
Every expected-result comparison is independent of reusing the query itself as the oracle.

reviewPrompts: Why can COUNT(*) and COUNT(temperature_c) disagree?
When does a filter belong in HAVING instead of WHERE?
How would an accidental many-to-many join distort an otherwise correct average?

lessons.title: Preserve provenance while rejecting bad data
objectives: Write a small validation policy that distinguishes missing, malformed and duplicate records.
Trace every accepted or rejected row to a source filename and row number.
Reconcile input, accepted and rejected counts without silently discarding evidence.

topics.title: Input contracts
details: Required fields, allowed NULL temperature, numeric ranges and reference validity.
An identical repeated ID is still a duplicate to report under the chosen first-valid-row policy.

topics.title: Provenance and explicit rejection
details: Preserve the raw input, source filename, CSV data-row number and rejection reason.
Do not fabricate replacements for missing values or include employer data in a learning fixture.

topics.title: Reconciliation
details: Every input data row receives exactly one outcome.
Reconcile counts first, then check that validated query totals still match the clean fixture.

assignment.title: Account for all ten rows in a dirty fixture
instructions: Budget about 135 minutes. Export the six original clean readings to a learner-authored CSV, representing the allowed missing temperature as an empty field.

Append four rows in this order: an exact duplicate of r2; r7 with station S9 and an otherwise valid reading; r8 with station S1 and temperature 'warm'; and a row with an empty reading_id but otherwise valid fields.

Implement a validator retaining the first valid occurrence of an ID and recording later duplicates. Use distinct reasons DUPLICATE_ID, UNKNOWN_STATION, INVALID_TEMPERATURE and MISSING_ID for the four appended cases.
Write accepted rows and a rejection report with original values, filename and 1-based data-row number excluding the header. Do not modify the raw CSV.
Load only accepted rows into a fresh SQLite database and rerun the clean-fixture summary. Keep the source and counts in a small provenance manifest.
deliverables: Ten-row synthetic source CSV and its data contract.
Validator, accepted output, rejection report and provenance manifest.
A row-count reconciliation and clean-summary comparison.

Each of the four appended rows has the specified reason and the correct source data-row number.
The allowed missing temperature on r3 remains missing and does not become zero or a rejection.
Accepted query counts and means match the preceding lesson, and the raw input remains byte-for-byte unchanged.

reviewPrompts: What evidence is lost if you simply drop malformed rows?
Why should duplicate handling be a written policy rather than an incidental dictionary overwrite?
What can reconciled row counts prove, and what can they not prove?

modules.title: 04. Decomposition, complexity and basic data structures
modules.description: Practice bounded algorithmic reasoning in Python. Cover simple search, operation counts and basic container choices, not an interview-problem catalog, advanced graph algorithms or a second programming language.

lessons.title: Decompose a search problem and count its work
objectives: State search preconditions and a loop invariant in plain language.
Implement linear and iterative binary search with the same observable contract.
Compare operation growth separately from noisy wall-clock timing.

topics.title: From problem to algorithm
details: Specify input, output, edge cases and the meaning of not found before implementation.
Separate correctness, termination and efficiency; binary search requires an ordered input.

topics.title: Growth rates
details: Constant, logarithmic, linear and quadratic growth as introductory models.
Choose a countable operation; best and worst cases need different input examples.

topics.title: Bounded comparisons
details: Compare reference and alternative algorithms on the same inputs.
Do not claim a universal speedup from one timing run or ignore the cost of sorting an unsorted input.

video.locator: CS50x 2025 Week 3 - Algorithms: Linear Search, Binary Search and Asymptotic Notation. Translate the ideas into Python; do not undertake the C problem set.

reading.locator: Chapter 2 Algorithm Analysis: section 2.2 What Is Algorithm Analysis? and section 2.3 Big O Notation. Focus on operation counting and constant/logarithmic/linear/quadratic comparisons.

assignment.title: Compare two searches with a transparent counter
instructions: Budget about 120 minutes. Implement linear_search and iterative binary_search, each returning an index or None, plus the number of inspected list elements.
State that binary_search expects an ascending list. Do not insert sorting or an extra linear sortedness check into its measured search loop; discuss those costs separately.
Check an empty list, one-element hit and miss, first and last positions, an interior hit, an absent target and a list containing duplicates. Any matching index is acceptable for duplicates.
For sorted unique lists of lengths 16, 32 and 64, search for a value larger than every element and count inspections.
Write the invariant and termination argument in at most 200 words, and explain why operation counts are not milliseconds.
deliverables: Two search functions and at least eight correctness checks.
An inspection-count table for lengths 16, 32 and 64.
A short invariant, termination and complexity explanation.
acceptanceCriteria: Both implementations find valid matching indices or return None consistently with a simple membership oracle.
Empty input requires zero element inspections.
The absent-above-maximum linear searches inspect 16, 32 and 64 elements; binary searches inspect at most 5, 6 and 7 respectively.
The explanation states the sorted-input precondition and does not claim that sorting is free or that one measured timing proves an asymptotic bound.

reviewPrompts: Which fact about the remaining search interval stays true after every binary-search step?
How does a precondition differ from an invariant?
Why might a linear method still be reasonable for a tiny or one-off unsorted input?

lessons.title: Choose structures by the operations they must support
objectives: Demonstrate FIFO and LIFO behavior with Python containers.
Use a dictionary for identity lookup and a set for distinct membership.
Explain an average-case efficiency benefit without promising worst-case constant time.

topics.title: Abstract behavior
details: A stack specifies last-in-first-out behavior; a queue specifies first-in-first-out behavior.
An abstract data type describes operations and invariants, not one mandatory implementation.

topics.title: Python implementations
details: Use list.append/pop for a stack and collections.deque for queue endpoints.
Use dictionaries for keyed records and sets for membership; distinguish average-case hash lookup from a worst-case guarantee.

topics.title: State consistency
details: Keep queue order and ID lookup consistent without dropping duplicate-input evidence silently.
Define empty-container behavior and avoid mutating a list while iterating over it.

reading.locator: Tutorial chapter 5 Data Structures: 5.1.1 Using Lists as Stacks, 5.1.2 Using Lists as Queues, 5.4 Sets and 5.5 Dictionaries.

assignment.title: Model a five-item local work queue
instructions: Budget about 135 minutes. Build a small function-based queue model for five invented task IDs using deque for order and a dictionary for their descriptions.
Enqueue T1, T2 and T3; process two; enqueue T4 and T5; then process the rest. A separate list records processed IDs as a stack that can show the most recently processed item.
Reject a repeated ID explicitly rather than silently replacing its description. Keep a set of IDs seen during this bounded run.
Define an explicit empty-queue outcome and check it. Keep the entire exercise local and in memory; it is not a concurrent job service.
Write a table matching enqueue, dequeue, last-processed lookup and duplicate detection to their container and expected operation cost.
deliverables: Function-based model, operation trace and checks.
Container/operation decision table.
A short explanation of the model's invariants and limits.
acceptanceCriteria: Processing order is T1, T2, T3, T4, T5 for the specified sequence.
The processed stack's last item is T5, and reversing it gives LIFO order without changing the queue's FIFO contract.
A duplicate ID is reported and does not change the accepted task count or stored description.
The empty case is explicit, queue and lookup state remain consistent, and no list.pop(0) is used as the queue implementation.

reviewPrompts: Which operations make a deque a better queue than a Python list?
When would a dictionary be inappropriate as the sole representation of a queue?
What state must stay consistent when one task is removed?

modules.title: 05. Git, tests, debugging and reproducibility
modules.description: Make small programs inspectable and repeatable. Use a disposable local Git repository, standard-library tests and explicit run evidence. No remote account, hosted CI, container platform or deployment is necessary.

lessons.title: Explain and preserve a local change history
objectives: Distinguish working-tree changes, staged changes and committed snapshots.
Create and merge a branch and resolve a small intentional conflict.
Undo an unwanted behavior through a new explicit change without rewriting shared history.

topics.title: Git's model
details: Snapshots, commits, parents, branches and the staging area.
status, diff, staged diff and log answer different questions.

topics.title: Small reviewable changes
details: Commit one coherent intent at a time and write a message explaining why.
Ignore generated outputs and environments; ignoring a file does not remove an already tracked copy.

topics.title: Safe collaboration concepts
details: A merge reconciles histories; conflict markers require an intentional resolution.
For this beginner exercise use new corrective commits, not force pushes, hard resets or modifications to another repository.

assignment.title: Create a reviewable history in a throwaway repository
instructions: Budget about 120 minutes. Initialize a new disposable local repository containing a copy of one original Foundation exercise. Do not use an employer or existing portfolio repository.
Use per-command Git identity options with an invented learner name and learner@example.invalid if identity is needed; do not change a global profile or create a remote account.
Create at least four coherent commits, showing status, unstaged diff, staged diff and log at appropriate points. Ignore the virtual environment and generated output before committing.
Create a branch, make different edits to the same disposable documentation line on the two branches, merge and resolve the intended conflict.
Introduce and then correct a small documentation mistake in a new commit. Explain how this preserves history instead of concealing the earlier change.

Before/after conflict resolution evidence.
A short explanation of staged versus unstaged changes and the corrective commit.
acceptanceCriteria: At least four meaningful commits exist, with a resolved branch merge and a separate corrective commit visible in history.
No conflict markers remain in the final file.
Environment directories, generated data and secrets are absent from tracked files.
The learner identifies what each of status, diff and staged diff shows, without changing a global identity or publishing the repository.

reviewPrompts: Why can the working file differ from both the staged version and the last commit?
What does a branch name point to?
Why is adding a filename to .gitignore insufficient after it was committed?

lessons.title: Turn a failure into a regression test
objectives: Write independent tests for normal, boundary and invalid-input behavior.
Reproduce a bug with a small failing case before changing the implementation.
Demonstrate that a test detects a deliberately reintroduced fault.

topics.title: Test design
details: Arrange, act and assert; an oracle must not simply repeat the implementation.
Check values, shapes, types, exceptions and input mutation where the contract makes them observable.

topics.title: Standard-library testing
details: unittest.TestCase, test methods, assertEqual, assertRaises and discovery.
Learn only the minimal class/self syntax needed to organize tests, not a full object-oriented design syllabus.

topics.title: Debugging loop
details: Observe, minimize, hypothesize, inspect, correct and rerun.
A passing suite is evidence about covered cases, not a proof of every possible behavior.

assignment.title: Protect the duration parser and observation summary
instructions: Budget about 165 minutes. Add a unittest suite for the original duration parser and collection summarizer, with at least twelve named tests.
Cover successful values, both parser bounds, malformed input, empty records, allowed None, legitimate zero and unchanged inputs.
Deliberately change one comparison boundary or incorrectly filter out zero in a disposable working copy. Capture the failing test, minimize the cause and repair the implementation.
Reintroduce the same fault briefly to show the regression test fails for the intended reason, then restore the correct implementation.
Run the suite through unittest discovery and write a concise bug note separating the symptom, cause, fix and remaining uncertainty.
deliverables: At least twelve named automated tests and the corrected implementation.
A red/green execution record showing the specific regression.
A short bug explanation with one explicitly uncovered risk.
acceptanceCriteria: At least twelve tests are discovered and cover the listed normal, boundary and invalid cases.
The deliberately reintroduced fault causes at least one relevant test to fail; a test that always passes is not accepted.
After correction, the tests pass without suppressing exceptions or changing expected values merely to match faulty code.
The suite is local and deterministic, with no network, clock or private-data dependency.

reviewPrompts: How can a test contain the same bug as the implementation?
Why is a smaller failing example often more useful than a longer error log?
What evidence shows that a new test actually protects against the reported bug?

lessons.title: Recreate a result from recorded inputs and commands
objectives: Record the source revision, interpreter, dependencies and input identity needed for a rerun.
Recreate a small tool in a second fresh environment without hidden notebook state.
Compare stable data outputs while separating volatile run metadata.

Record no third-party runtime dependencies explicitly when that is true; do not invent a dependency lockfile's guarantees.

topics.title: Environment isolation
details: Recreate an environment instead of copying its platform-specific directory.
Avoid unrecorded global packages, absolute personal paths, ambient state and undeclared network access.

topics.title: Deterministic evidence
details: Sort report records and use explicit encoding and output conventions.
A stable hash identifies bytes, not their truth or permission to use them; volatile timestamps belong outside equality-checked data.

assignment.title: Run the same small report in two clean environments

Prepare a second clean copy with a newly created virtual environment, not a copied environment folder. Run the documented commands without relying on an open notebook session.
Compare the canonical data output and test outcomes. Keep environment paths, timestamps and other volatile observations in a separate run log.
Change one input byte in a disposable copy and show that input identity changes. Do not assert that the hash proves the dataset is accurate or legally reusable.

Two real execution logs and a data-output comparison.
An input-change/hash observation and known portability limitations.

The manifest identifies code revision and input bytes, not just an informal project name.
Tests run in both environments without undeclared third-party packages or network access.
A changed input produces a different recorded SHA-256 hash, and any environment-specific setup differences are documented honestly.

What does an input hash establish, and what does it not establish?
Why should you recreate a virtual environment rather than commit and copy it?

modules.title: 06. Numerical and statistical reasoning
modules.description: Develop numeracy, honest summaries and elementary probability/sampling intuition using small synthetic data and Python. No calculus, finance, machine learning, formal inference course or R installation is required.

lessons.title: Keep units, percentages and numeric precision honest
objectives: Convert units and distinguish percentage-point changes from relative percentage changes.
Demonstrate a floating-point representation discrepancy without calling it a Python defect.
Choose an explicit comparison tolerance or exact representation for a stated need.

topics.title: Numeracy and units
details: Ratios, fractions, proportions, percentages, scientific notation and consistent units.
A denominator and baseline must be named; absolute and relative changes answer different questions.

topics.title: Representations
details: Integer counts, binary floating-point approximations and exact decimal construction from strings.
Rounding a display does not repair or change the underlying mathematical model.

topics.title: Comparisons and boundaries
details: Absolute versus relative tolerance, especially near zero.
Reject nonfinite values when a measurement contract requires finite numbers; precision is not the same thing as measurement accuracy.

assignment.title: Audit a miniature measurement summary
instructions: Budget about 90 minutes. Produce a short Python-backed worksheet converting 90000 milliseconds to seconds and 12 accepted observations out of 20 into a percentage.
Compare a change from 60 percent to 75 percent using both percentage points and relative percent change, naming the baseline.
Compare 0.7 + 0.2 with 0.9 using direct equality, displayed rounding, math.isclose and Decimal values constructed from strings. Explain the different questions these comparisons answer.

Define a small measurement comparator with an explicitly documented absolute tolerance near zero and a relative tolerance away from zero. Include one acceptable and one unacceptable difference for each.
Add checks that nonfinite measurements are rejected. Do not use decimal arithmetic as a claim about instrument accuracy.

Comparator function and at least six checks.
A table naming units, denominator, baseline and representation choices.
acceptanceCriteria: The conversions give 90 seconds and 60 percent; the change is 15 percentage points and 25 percent relative to the original 60 percent.
The floating-point and Decimal observations are recorded from an actual run and explained as representation behavior.
Near-zero comparison uses an explicit nonzero absolute tolerance, and both accepted and rejected differences are checked.
NaN and infinite values do not silently pass as valid measurements.

reviewPrompts: Why are percentage points and percent change not interchangeable?
When is exact integer representation preferable to a floating-point value?
Why does relative tolerance alone often fail near zero?

lessons.title: Describe a distribution, not just its average
objectives: Calculate and interpret mean, median, spread and missing-value counts.
Show how one outlier can change a mean without changing the median.
Label sample versus population variance and state a quartile convention.

topics.title: Center and shape
details: Mean, median, mode, distribution shape, dot plots and histograms.
A numeric-looking identifier is not automatically a meaningful measurement.

topics.title: Spread
details: Range, variance, standard deviation, quartiles and interquartile range.
Sample and population variance use different denominators; quartile conventions can differ between tools.

topics.title: Honest reporting
details: Always report units, sample size and missingness alongside summaries.
Outliers and skewness can make a single average misleading; descriptive association is not a causal explanation.

assignment.title: Explain two five-value summaries
instructions: Budget about 120 minutes. Use the original synthetic durations [4,4,5,7,10] seconds. Calculate count, mean, median, range and sample variance by hand and independently with Python.
Replace the final value 10 with 50 and compare the mean and median. Add a separate None entry and show the difference between raw count and measured count.
Calculate quartiles using a clearly stated method. For a by-hand method you may exclude the central observation before taking the medians of the lower and upper halves.
Draw a labelled dot plot or small histogram, by hand or as text; plotting packages are not required.
Write a 150-word interpretation naming the population you cannot infer from this deliberately tiny synthetic sample.

A labelled plot plus a compact summary table.
An interpretation with missingness, units and limitations.

After replacing 10 with 50, the mean is 14 and the median remains 5.
Adding None increases raw count but not measured count and does not insert a zero into the average.
The quartile convention is stated, sample variance is not labelled population variance, and the conclusion makes no causal or population-wide claim.

Why do standard deviation and variance have different units?
How would you explain a disagreement between two software packages' quartiles?

lessons.title: Separate chance, sampling variability and bias
objectives: Enumerate a small sample space and calculate simple event probabilities.
Distinguish independent draws from draws whose probabilities change after an observation.
Demonstrate sampling variability and explain why a fixed random seed does not eliminate bias.

topics.title: Elementary probability
details: Sample spaces, events, complements, addition/OR and multiplication/AND.
Conditioning changes the relevant sample space; disjoint events and independent events are different concepts.

topics.title: Sampling
details: Population, sample, parameter, statistic, simple random selection and convenience sampling.
Larger samples can reduce random variation without repairing a systematically biased selection rule.

topics.title: Simulation with limits
details: Use a local random.Random instance with a recorded seed for reproducible demonstrations.
Simulation frequencies are observations, not exact probabilities or guaranteed closeness; pseudorandom simulation is not secret generation.

assignment.title: Enumerate first, simulate second
instructions: Budget about 150 minutes. Create ten distinct labelled tokens, three red and seven blue. Enumerate ordered pairs with replacement and ordered pairs without replacement.
Calculate the probability that both tokens are red in each model. Explain how observing a red first draw changes the second-draw probability without replacement.

Simulate 10000 two-token draws for each model using a recorded local seed. Report frequencies and differences from the enumerated probabilities, without imposing a brittle exact-match requirement on random output.
Use the synthetic population of integers 0 through 59. Compare the mean of the first ten values with five separate simple random samples of ten values.
Repeat one seeded run to demonstrate reproducibility and write a short explanation of why a reproducible convenience sample is still biased.
deliverables: Two exact enumeration tables or counts and a probability explanation.
Simulation and sampling code with recorded seeds.
Observed-frequency and sample-mean tables with a bias/variability discussion.
acceptanceCriteria: The with-replacement enumeration has 100 ordered pairs, 9 with two red tokens; the without-replacement enumeration has 90 ordered pairs, 6 with two red tokens.
The stated probabilities are 9/100 and 1/15 respectively; the explanation distinguishes the two sampling mechanisms.
The population mean is 29.5 and the first-ten mean is 4.5; random sample means are measured rather than invented.
The same seed and runtime reproduce the same simulated sequence, while all reported frequencies remain in the valid probability range.
The write-up does not claim that more trials repair the convenience-sampling rule or guarantee a particular random error bound.

reviewPrompts: How does sampling without replacement change conditional probability?
What is the difference between sampling variability and bias?
Why does reproducibility not make a dataset representative?

modules.title: 07. HTTP, privacy and responsible AI-assisted work

lessons.title: Read an HTTP response and validate its data
objectives: Explain the roles of DNS, host, port, method, status, headers and body at an introductory level.
Fetch and decode a small JSON response with a finite timeout.
Distinguish a successful empty result from an HTTP, transport or parse failure.

details: Names resolve to addresses; clients contact a host and port and exchange requests and responses.
URL parts, GET versus state-changing intent, status codes, content type and HTTPS transport protection.

topics.title: JSON and Python
details: JSON text is not a Python object until parsed; validate the expected shape and value types after parsing.
Use urllib.request and json for this bounded standard-library client; a provider-specific SDK is unnecessary.

topics.title: Failure and scope
details: Distinguish HTTPError, URLError/transport failure and JSON decoding errors.
The local teaching server is not production infrastructure; bind only to loopback and serve only synthetic fixtures.

assignment.title: Inspect a localhost JSON fixture and three failures
instructions: Budget about 150 minutes. In a new fixtures directory create good.json containing an object with station_id S1 and values [18,20], plus bad.json containing deliberately invalid JSON.
Start Python's http.server on an unused local port, bound to 127.0.0.1 and restricted to this fixtures directory. Do not expose it publicly or serve a home directory.

Explain where HTTPS would matter for a real remote connection and why this loopback HTTP exercise is not a deployment pattern.

One successful response record and three distinct failure observations.
A request/response diagram and a short transport/privacy explanation.

limitations: This is an actual Common Foundation curriculum: 8 ordered modules and 22 lessons, not a union of advanced Data/SDE/Quant/AI specializations. Advanced calculus, finance, deep learning, professional backend/distributed design, cloud operations and specialist SDE source families are intentionally excluded.

Prior exposure to tools is not independently demonstrated proficiency. Initialize every module, lesson, assignment and review as not started/incomplete with no score, completion date or invented result. Meeting future acceptance criteria is a completion gate, not an assertion that the learner has already met it.

The lesson estimates total 5430 minutes, or 90.5 hours. These are personal planning estimates including the explicitly budgeted assignment work, selected lecture viewing, reading and recall. They are not measured learner timings or guarantees. Repeated targeted viewing is budgeted, not another full-course enrollment; optional full lectures, extra exercises, setup obstacles and remediation can require additional time.

All assignments, synthetic fixtures, acceptance criteria and review prompts in this handoff are original. Expected values are small-fixture oracles, not observed learner outcomes. Third-party problem statements, solutions, exam questions, book chapters and transcripts are not copied. Optional questions arrays are deliberately empty.

All external research used unauthenticated public HTML, JSON or text-source HTTP. Video titles, official topic locators and player links were verified, but playback, current regional availability, captions and future embed behavior were not end-to-end tested. Videos are strictly link/embed-only with downloadUrl null; offer the official page link if a provider blocks embedding.

No PDFs or media were downloaded. Every downloadUrl is null: no direct PDF artifact was checked for a hosting-ready edition. Permitted redistribution records concern verified licenses for covered text/documentation, not an already downloaded or fully audited offline asset bundle.

The field redistribution=permitted is conditional source permission, not an instruction to turn on hosting. Apply each sources.permissionEvidence deploymentGate first. While deployment purpose is unknown, keep NC-licensed Think Python text, Pro Git and the Runestone algorithms book link-only in the application; do not assume an educational, free-to-user or advertising-supported product is noncommercial.

Think Python text and code have different licenses. Database Design has a separately licensed cover photograph. OpenIntro excludes covers, branding and other categories from its general grant and limits derivative branding. GNU Bash requires GFDL notice/source/modification compliance. Python prose is PSF-licensed, not all 0BSD. Preserve these distinctions when adapting the catalog.

Technical Writing Essentials remains whole-resource link-only because its official metadata lists third-party restrictions and unresolved ownership, including an image in the assigned scope chapter. No whole-book/PDF hosting clearance is claimed. Crash Course episodes and the specific How to Speak upload also have no verified open redistribution grant in this handoff.

Bash and CS50 C-based demonstrations are used only for shared concepts. Windows learners should use an installed Bash environment or deliberate PowerShell equivalents; no profile or execution-policy change is required. Algorithms are implemented in Python, and the pytest lecture is paired with explicit unittest reading rather than misrepresented as a unittest tutorial.

The SQL textbook contains SQL Server-specific examples and some conceptual simplifications. SQLite official references and Python's bound-parameter interface govern the executable labs. Foreign-key enforcement must be enabled per connection before inserts. No PostgreSQL manual was needed or researched for this handoff.

The statistics book has optional R-based supplements, and Think Python offers optional Colab notebooks. Neither is required: all assigned computation uses original local Python exercises. Public lectures and readings are free; optional hosted feedback, saved interactive progress, certificates or paid print editions are not part of completion criteria.

HTTP work is a tiny loopback-only teaching lab, not a production server or a robust external-API integration. Official Python manual sections are used for library behavior rather than treating historical RFC references as current protocol standards. Privacy and AI-assistance lessons are basic professional hygiene, not certification, comprehensive security review or proof of model reliability.

The portfolio build briefs are scope/context only. No SDE A/B mapping is appropriated, projectMappings is intentionally empty, and the final synthetic integration exercise is not claimed as one of the user's completed historical projects or planned advanced resume projects. No employer code/data, accounts, real credentials, private reports or biometric assets are required.

Use canonicalConceptTags and the foundation-prefixed lesson IDs as the shared prerequisite/progress references in later tracks. Reusing a prerequisite should reuse this lesson's actual future progress, not duplicate it or auto-complete it from a job title.
Successful completion can provide evidence of these bounded prerequisites; it does not guarantee employment, an examination result, profitability, expert mastery or production readiness.
